paras: The threatened lynching of George Lenhart took place in August 1882 in and around Evansville, Indiana, after Lenhart, a German laborer, was arrested in the murder of saloon keeper Alexander Wieber, his wife and their young son. A vigilance committee was organized and men were reported gathering to lynch him, but the sheriff moved him to the jail at Boonville in Warrick County. In December 1882 Lenhart was discharged when the State attorney could not make a case, and a German-language paper cited the affair as proof that innocent men could fall victim to lynch law.

Early on Sunday, August 13, 1882, a beer driver named Löffler found Wieber, his wife and their son killed in the family's saloon and home in the northwestern part of Evansville, with an infant of about six months unharmed in its crib. The house had belonged to a man named Krugg, who had been killed there about six years earlier; his widow had leased it to Wieber and then married Lenhart, who wanted the house for himself. According to the wire reports, Lenhart had been heard to threaten to kill Wieber if he did not leave, and the Illinois Staats-Zeitung added that Wieber had thrown him out of the saloon a few days before.

Police arrested Lenhart along with Charles W. Carter, Philip Voll and a young man named Jo Bird, but suspicion pointed most strongly to Lenhart, who denied his guilt. A St. Landry Democrat account said footprints leading from the house matched Lenhart's habit of walking with one shoe off because of a sore foot. A dispatch of August 14 offered another lead, reporting that two Black men had been seen rowing rapidly downstream that morning and were followed by a detective.

Because many people called for Lenhart to be lynched, Sheriff Kerth moved him 'in the silence of night' to the jail at Booneville, a step that angered citizens in the lower part of Evansville. On August 16, the day of a funeral at which thousands viewed the bodies and Father Bultman cautioned against mob law, a rumor spread that a large body of men was gathering in German township to ride to Booneville and lynch him. The dispatch added that telegraph wires to Booneville were not working, but no report of an attack on the jail appears in the coverage.

A coroner's jury later found that Lenhart had killed Alexander Wieber with premeditated malice on the morning of August 13. After a trial of several days, however, he was discharged on December 18, 1882, when the State attorney declared himself unable to make a case. The Illinois Staats-Zeitung reported that his innocence had been shown, that the acquittal was greeted with loud applause, and that there was talk of compensating him for his imprisonment.

English-language papers carried the case as wire copy, from the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer's 'A Brace of Tragedies' to a short December notice in the Morning Journal and Courier. The August dispatches dwelt on the 'fiendish' killings and reported that 'the people seem to be determined that Lenhart must hang' without comment.

German-language papers in Chicago and Baltimore followed the case more closely, since the victims and the accused were German. The Illinois Staats-Zeitung closed the story with an editorial note that innocent people too could become victims of 'Judge Lynch', saying Lenhart had been suspected on nothing more than a few empty threats.

Reports differed on motive: the first dispatches said nothing of value was taken and money remained in a locked drawer, while a later dispatch said a watch, two pistols, pocket books and money were stolen.

bases: Crowds demanded and organized to lynch George Lenhart, a German accused of a triple murder, and the sheriff moved him to another county's jail to prevent it (A17, A20, A25, A26).

Lenhart was not killed: a vigilance committee and a reported body of men sought to lynch him for the accused murder, but he was moved to the Boonville jail and later discharged (A17, A25, A26); the papers identify him as a German, not a Black man (A20, A22).

The threat to lynch Lenhart and his removal to another county's jail are reported independently by an Evansville wire dispatch (A17), the Illinois Staats-Zeitung (A20, A26) and a December dispatch (A25).
